tagline: Latin America's largest port has the busiest little ferry crossing in the world — 400 metres of water that move more than 36,000 people and vehicles a day, now backed by a state contract that mandates an electric fleet.
summary: Santos and Guarujá face each other across the mouth of the Port of Santos, Latin America's largest port. The road between them is a 45 km, 50-minute detour; the water between them is 400 metres. So the water already won: the state balsa crossing carries 21,000+ vehicles and some 15,000 walk-on and cycle-on riders every day, a second 24-hour launch line links Santos Centro to Vicente de Carvalho, and around them sit a million-passenger cruise terminal, yacht-club marinas, boat-only beaches and a mangrove canal. In November 2025 São Paulo state signed a 20-year, R$2.5 billion concession that explicitly requires 40+ new vessels — most of them fully electric — across these crossings. This is a market where water transit is an adopted habit, the regulator has already mandated electrification, and the missing layer is exactly what foiling provides: speed, smoothness and direct routes the flat-deck ferries were never designed to fly.

demand_signals.label: The world's highest-volume crossing of its kind
demand_signals.value: ≈21,000 vehicles + ≈7,600 pedestrians + ≈7,700 cyclists per day on the 400 m Santos–Guarujá balsa
demand_signals.note: A seven-minute, 24-hour crossing that outperforms a 45 km road detour — proof the water is the main street here

demand_signals.label: A regulated, measured system
demand_signals.value: 9.65M users in H1 2024 on the litoral crossings; ≈11M passengers + 10M vehicles/yr across the 14 crossings in the state system
demand_signals.note: São Paulo's Sistema de Travessias runs 34 vessels moving 57,000+ people and vehicles daily — official, countable, state-published demand
demand_signals.source: G1 Santos e Região (Jul 2024); UOL/Governo de SP (Nov 2025)

demand_signals.label: An electric-fleet mandate already signed
demand_signals.value: R$2.5bn, 20-year PPP (Acqua Vias SP, Nov 2025) requiring 40+ new vessels, most 100% electric, 20 modernised terminals, ~18,000 t CO₂/yr saved
demand_signals.note: First project in Brazil certified by the OECD's Blue Dot Network — the authority has formally specified clean, quiet water transit; the design-in window is open now

demand_signals.label: A million cruise passengers at one pier
demand_signals.value: ≈1,000,000 passengers and 152 ship calls forecast for the 2024/25 season at the Concais terminal
demand_signals.note: South America's biggest cruise gateway sits inside the harbour — and every premium onward transfer to Guarujá's beaches and marinas today goes 45 km by road

demand_signals.label: A metro-scale summer market
demand_signals.value: Up to 18.3M tourists expected on the Baixada Santista coast in the 2025/26 summer season; Santos alone expects 3.5M+, Guarujá ≈1.5M
demand_signals.note: São Paulo city and its 20M+ people are 80 km up the highway — and the highway is the bottleneck

demand_signals.label: Latin America's largest port as the backdrop
demand_signals.value: Record 179.8M tonnes handled in 2024; 5.4M TEU — the region's #1 container port
demand_signals.note: A dense maritime-services economy (pilots, agents, surveyors, terminal executives) that moves across the channel every working day

use_cases.title: Foiling overlay on the busiest crossing in Brazil
use_cases.body: Scheduled N35 Shuttle headways alongside the balsa on Santos–Guarujá and Santos Centro–Vicente de Carvalho: seated, enclosed, smooth across the port-channel chop, and aligned with the concession's own electric-fleet requirement. The habit exists — tens of thousands cross daily; the upgrade is speed, comfort and reliability, not persuasion.

use_cases.title: Cruise-to-beach in minutes, not an hour by road
use_cases.body: Direct transfers from the Concais cruise terminal to the Guarujá shore — the balsa head, Porto Marina Astúrias, and boat-only Praia do Góes — replacing the 45 km highway loop for a million seasonal passengers, plus water excursions to Ilha das Palmas and the Bertioga mangrove canal.

use_cases.title: The port economy's water shuttle
use_cases.body: Latin America's largest port lines both banks of the channel: terminal operators, shipping agencies, pilots and inspectors move between Santos, Vicente de Carvalho and the Guarujá bank all day. A quiet, fast corporate shuttle turns those crossings into minutes — with the Iate Clube de Santos base and the marinas as natural nodes.

use_cases.title: Marina-to-marina weekends
use_cases.body: Porto Marina Astúrias, the Iate Clube de Santos, Marina Dolfin and the private club island of Ilha das Palmas form a compact leisure triangle in Santos Bay — silent foiling hops between marinas, beach coves and the club island, and a scenic run up the Canal de Bertioga behind Santo Amaro island.

journeys.today: A 12-minute displacement launch across 2,200 m of working-port water, on vessels the state is only now beginning to renew — or a long bus ride around.
journeys.with_navier: A five-minute foiling glide above the channel chop, seated and dry, on the exact corridor the new concession has earmarked for electric vessels.

journeys.today: Disembark from a cruise ship, then take a taxi 45 km around the estuary by highway — the water route your ship just used is not offered to you.
journeys.with_navier: Step off the ship and foil straight down the harbour to Guarujá's marina in minutes, past the working port — the arrival becomes the excursion.

journeys.from: Ponte Edgard Perdigão (Ponta da Praia, Santos)
journeys.today: A queue for a small open launch across the harbour mouth to a beach that has no road at all.
journeys.with_navier: A silent, zero-wake hop to the boat-only beach — more departures, no diesel fumes over the sand.

journeys.to: Bertioga balsa head (via Canal de Bertioga)
journeys.today: Either a slow cruise through the canal or a long drive around via the highway; the mangrove canal behind Santo Amaro island is mostly left to fishing boats.
journeys.with_navier: A ~17 nm flight up the port channel and through the mangrove-lined canal to Bertioga — the region's most beautiful waterway turned into a usable link.

journeys.today: The balsa is honest and cheap — and from H2 2026 free for pedestrians — but it is a flat-deck vehicle ferry: you wait for the ramp, share the deck with 40 cars, and cross at walking pace when swell and tide allow.
journeys.with_navier: A premium express alongside the free ferry: direct, seated, minutes-not-queues, running to the marinas and piers the balsa was never built to serve. The pitch is time and comfort — the balsa keeps doing its job.

navier_fit.pioneer_ii: The entire market sits inside a ~17 nm envelope — the crossing pairs (0.2–1.2 nm), the cruise-terminal and marina spurs (1–4 nm), Ilha das Palmas and Praia do Góes hops (0.3–2 nm), and the Canal de Bertioga run (~17 nm) — trivially within the 70 nm all-electric range, with marina charging at Porto Marina Astúrias and the Iate Clube de Santos as the natural backbone. Zero wake matters here: the estuary holds fishing communities (Ilha Diana, Santa Cruz dos Navegantes) and mangrove margins.
navier_fit.quanta_lr: Quanta-LR's 700 nm hybrid range opens the coastal line-hauls beyond the estuary: São Paulo's north coast (Ilhabela/São Sebastião, another crossing in the same state concession) and onward up the Costa Verde to Paraty, Angra dos Reis and Rio de Janeiro — linking this market into the existing Angra–Ilha Grande network, with no charging-infrastructure dependency en route.

competitive_landscape: The water is already the main street, run by the state: the Santos–Guarujá balsa (19 vessels on the crossing's fleet, 24h, ~7 min) and the Santos–Vicente de Carvalho lancha line (24h, ~12 min) moved 9.65M users in H1 2024, alongside traditional catraia small-boat operators, the municipal Ilha Diana boat, and private launches to Praia do Góes. From 2026 the system passes to the Acqua Vias SP consortium under a 20-year PPP that mandates a mostly-electric new fleet — the strongest possible demand evidence: the authority has measured the ridership, priced the system, and specified clean water transit in a signed contract. What no operator offers today is speed, smoothness or direct point-to-point service to the marinas, beaches and the cruise pier. One positioning note held honestly throughout: pedestrians ride the balsa free from H2 2026, so a premium service here sells minutes, comfort and routes — never a fare comparison with a free ferry. And the Santos–Guarujá road tunnel (contract signed Jan 2026, opening ~2031) will serve vehicles on one axis; beaches, islands, marinas and cruise transfers stay water-only, and the five-year construction window adds disruption the water layer can absorb.
seasonality: Austral summer (Dec–Mar) is peak: up to 18.3M seasonal tourists on the Baixada coast, and the cruise season runs Nov–Apr out of Concais. Winter (Jun–Aug) is mild and quieter but the crossings run 24h year-round — this is commuter demand, not just leisure. The operational hook: South Atlantic cold fronts and strong tides periodically disrupt the flat-deck balsas (crossing suspensions and long queues make local news), and the estuary chop makes small-launch rides wet and slow — foiling flies above exactly that. No cyclone exposure; the estuary and canal are sheltered water, with the harbour mouth and Santos Bay legs the only open-water exposure.
regulatory_note: A single, sophisticated authority stack: the Departamento Hidroviário de São Paulo (DH, under Semil) owns the crossings; from 2026 the Acqua Vias SP consortium operates them under a 20-year PPP whose contract requires 40+ new vessels (predominantly electric), 20 modernised terminals and ~18,000 t CO₂/yr in savings — the first Brazilian project certified under the OECD's Blue Dot Network. Vessel class and crew sit with the Capitania dos Portos (Brazilian Navy); waterway passenger services with ANTAQ; and the Autoridade Portuária de Santos governs channel traffic in Latin America's busiest box-port approach. For a foiling fleet this is a design-in market: the electrification requirement is already law-of-the-contract, and the state has shown (Hora Marcada paid booking) that it prices time.
signature_routes: Ponta da Praia ↔ Guarujá balsa head (the 400 m harbour-mouth crossing — the busiest of its kind in the world)
Santos Centro (Praça da República) ↔ Vicente de Carvalho (the regulated 24h commuter lancha line)
Concais cruise terminal ↔ Porto Marina Astúrias (cruise-to-marina premium arrival)
Ponte Edgard Perdigão ↔ Praia do Góes (the boat-only beach hop)
Ponta da Praia ↔ Bertioga via the Canal de Bertioga (the mangrove canal run behind Santo Amaro island)

precedents.where: Travessias Hídricas PPP (Acqua Vias SP, signed basis Nov 2025)
precedents.why_it_matters: The very market has already committed, in a 20-year contract, to a mostly-electric fleet on these exact crossings — clean, quiet water transit here is not a proposal, it is procurement.
Demonstrates electric foiling as the backbone of a national water-mobility network — the playbook for scaling from one marquee crossing to a full mesh.
